The court was therefore a place where speech was invited and controlled at once. People could speak, but their statements were examined by representatives of the king. Although the record does not reveal the methods used in each county, it does reveal an official expectation that testimony could be tested and converted into a ruling.

Seven groups of commissioners reported to the king on several counties. Each group included three or four noblemen, monks, and scribes. Rank, religious learning, and writing were joined in the process. A second group checked the details of the first a few weeks later, according to the account, as a safeguard against secret deals. Verification made the survey more than a collection of isolated reports. It gave the king a way to compare his servants and pursue consistency across England.

The work was written in Latin. The scribes’ notes were gathered and written into larger books, with the so-called Little Domesday and Exeter Domesday mentioned as possible examples. The account says that the final version may have been edited by one man, Samson of Winchester. The survey took little more than a year. Speed mattered because information that arrived too late could not serve the immediate purposes of taxation, settlement, and royal control. The achievement was administrative, but administration was not separate from compulsion. A rapid survey could make obligations legible before local claims had time to harden into resistance.

Domesday’s entries make inequality measurable in a way that Morgan’s account of the League does not. The survey says that William and his family personally owned about 17 per cent of all the land in England, while churchmen owned about 26 per cent. William’s tenants-in-chief held the rest. Most of those tenants had Norman names, though a handful of Englishmen appear to have retained their possessions after 1066. A few women landowners also appear, though not many. These figures portray a hierarchy produced in the aftermath of conquest, with land distributed through a ruling system and then recorded for its use.

A line in a land survey can carry the history of seizure without narrating the seizure itself. Ownership appears as a settled fact. The person who lost land may be reduced to an earlier holder, a name, or an omission. The recipient appears as a tenant-in-chief or landowner. The document is not a battlefield account, yet it belongs to a political order formed through war and maintained through obligations. It reveals the durable consequences of organised force more readily than the experiences that accompanied them.

For many towns and villages, the account says, Domesday is the first written record of their existence. That first appearance has an uneven character. A place becomes visible because the king needs to know what it contains and what it owes. Its inhabitants may be identified as free men or bondsmen; its land may be valued; its animals may be counted. The record gives a place administrative presence while placing it inside a hierarchy of ownership and service.

The population estimates drawn from Domesday range from one and a half million to more than three million, and some areas were not covered. Counting does not produce the same knowledge as witnessing. A survey can record obligations more reliably than fear, resentment, or private calculation. It can reveal a legal status without telling us how a person experienced that status. It can show that a king had the means to dispatch commissioners across England without telling us whether every community regarded the process as legitimate.

If the survey had been designed to measure aggression, it would have asked different questions. It might have recorded assaults, killings, threats, or raids. Instead, it asked who held land, who owed service, and what resources were available. Those questions still matter to a history of aggression because control over property and labour can be exercised without a direct assault. Coercion may be present in the ability to impose a judgment, demand a tax, or define a person as bound to a lord. The injury may take the form of deprivation, dependence, or the loss of a right rather than a wound visible on the body.

Domesday also prevents an easy opposition between force and administration. William’s victory at Hastings stands behind the survey’s authority, but the survey did not consist, in the passage we possess, of soldiers riding from village to village. It consisted of county courts, commissioners, monks, scribes, reports, checks, and books. A conquered kingdom could be governed through records. The record made power more durable by giving it categories and a memory. Violence may open a political order; writing may help it last.

Morgan’s account and Domesday bring different forms of order into the same question. Morgan describes a League whose political unity was expressed through nations, sachemships, hereditary succession, and family relationships. Domesday describes a royal survey that mapped land, status, taxes, and service after conquest. One cannot place fifty sachemships beside 17 per cent of English land and infer that one society was more or less aggressive. The sources answer different administrative and interpretive needs. They make different people visible.

Aggression is the broadest term available here, but breadth can become vagueness. It is useful to reserve it for behaviour, strategy, or action directed towards dominating, controlling, or harming another person or group. That direction may be physical, verbal, psychological, social, or structural. A threat can be aggressive without being violent in the narrower sense of physical force. An act can be instrumental, used to obtain land or obedience, or reactive, arising in response to provocation. The category identifies a family of actions aimed at imposing something on others, but it cannot function as a single historical measurement.

Anger belongs elsewhere. It is an internal state, ranging from irritation to rage, that may arise from perceived unfairness, threat, or frustration. A person can feel anger and refrain from aggression. Another can use aggression calmly to secure a goal. William’s commissioners, as the account presents them, acted through judgments, lists, and inspections; nothing in the record establishes their private emotional state. Morgan’s discussion of the League describes offices and kinship; it does not reveal whether a particular sachem felt anger while exercising authority. Separating feeling from action keeps an inferred emotion from becoming an observed event.

Injury names a consequence rather than a complete kind of action. Physical injury may result from an assault, a battle, an accident, punishment, or deprivation. Psychological injury may follow intimidation or confinement. Social injury may arise through exclusion, humiliation, or the destruction of relationships. The same injury can therefore emerge from different settings. A wound found in a burial is not by itself a classification of the act that caused it. A loss of land in a survey may be an outcome of conquest, a legal transfer, debt, or a disputed settlement, and the entry alone may not distinguish among them.

Interpersonal violence is narrower. It involves the intentional use of physical force or power by an individual or small group against other persons, with possible physical, sexual, or psychological harm, deprivation, or neglect. Violence can occur within families and households as well as between strangers. Control may be exerted through assault, stalking, sexual coercion, isolation, monitoring, or financial restriction. The direct scale is small, but its effects may be extensive. A household does not become a peaceful space simply because no army is present.

All violent acts are aggressive, but not all aggressive acts are violent. A verbal threat may seek to dominate without physical contact. An administrative decision may compel action through legal authority rather than immediate force. A land survey may classify a person as a bondsman and attach services to that status. Such acts should not be made equivalent to killing or torture. They should also not disappear from analysis merely because the source does not show a weapon.

Coercion describes the subversion of choice through threats, pressure, intimidation, or authority. Coercive law uses legal power to compel conduct or prevent a person from exercising a right. Its force may be immediate, as in a threat of punishment, or built into a relationship of dependence. Domesday offers an example of administrative coercion in the rule that disagreements were settled at once and could not be appealed. The source does not describe a physical act imposed on a named subject, but it records a system in which the king’s decision could close a dispute and establish an obligation.

Not every rule is equally coercive, and not every legal judgment is an act of aggression. A rule can coordinate conduct, settle competing claims, or protect a person from violence. The hereditary sachemships in Morgan’s account are evidence of an authority structure, not proof that every exercise of authority harmed someone. Political order can restrain private violence by providing procedures for disagreement. The same order can protect hierarchy and authorise punishment. Its effects have to be followed through particular rules and consequences.

Raiding has a more specific meaning. It is a rapid attack with a limited objective, often involving plunder, destruction, the capture of people, the release of prisoners, or the gathering of intelligence, followed by withdrawal rather than the permanent holding of territory. Raiding may occur within warfare, but it is not identical to warfare. A raid can be one operation carried out by a small force. Warfare refers to organised, large-scale armed conflict between political entities, such as states, confederations, or other organised communities. A society may conduct raids without sustaining a long campaign, and a war may contain raids without being reducible to them.

This distinction prevents the scale of an event from being confused with its purpose. A surprise attack on a settlement, a punitive expedition, and a battle for territory may all involve armed force, but they produce different patterns of risk and authority. The Iroquois passages supplied here do not describe any of them. Domesday records the political aftermath of a conquest and the administration of land, but it is not a military narrative. Warfare or raiding therefore remains unresolved in both sources.

Atrocity names a further category. Organised atrocity refers to large-scale, systematic violence against civilian populations. Genocide concerns acts committed with the intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial, or religious group. Crimes against humanity concern widespread or systematic attacks directed against a civilian population, including murder, torture, sexual violence, persecution, and enforced disappearance. War crimes are grave breaches of the laws and customs applicable in armed conflict. Ethnic cleansing describes the forced removal of an ethnic group from territory, often through force or intimidation, though the phrase is not itself a separate crime under international law.

These categories overlap without becoming synonyms. An atrocity can contain murder, deportation, sexual violence, enslavement, or destruction of homes. Warfare can produce atrocities, but not every act of warfare is an atrocity. Coercive law can inflict serious harm, but a tax assessment is not thereby genocide. Aggression can be present in all these settings while remaining too general to describe their organisation, scale, or legal character. The more severe the event, the more necessary it becomes to identify who acted, against whom, by what means, and under what authority.

That requirement answers the temptation to rank societies on a single line from peaceful to violent. The line promises simplicity. It might count deaths, injuries, battles, or recorded crimes and arrange periods according to a total. Yet injury, raiding, warfare, coercive administration, enslavement, deportation, and atrocity are not interchangeable units. A population may experience little recorded warfare and extensive domestic coercion. A state may reduce interpersonal violence while expanding conquest abroad. An administrative system may prevent some disputes and intensify the extraction of labour from others.

Institutions can enlarge harm because they connect decisions to resources, personnel, weapons, transport, records, and law. Domesday demonstrates a modest but important version of this principle. Seven groups of commissioners, aided by monks and scribes, could gather information across several counties, compare reports, and produce books in little more than a year. The same chain that made taxation more efficient could make an obligation harder to evade. The administrative form did not merely describe power. It helped power travel.

Institutions can also restrain. A council may prevent a personal quarrel from becoming a war. A hereditary office may create a rule of succession where seizure would otherwise be expected. A court may hear competing testimony and settle a claim rather than leave it to private force. Morgan’s description of the League gives us these possibilities without providing a particular case in which one occurred. Domesday provides judgments and verification without describing every consequence. Institutional capacity can organise harm or channel conflict, and the historian must follow the consequences rather than assign the institution a single moral character.

A distinction among aggression, injury, coercion, warfare, and atrocity changes what counts as evidence. To identify aggression, we look for directed action and its intended object. To identify injury, we examine the harm and its possible causes. To identify coercion, we ask how choice was constrained and what power backed the constraint. To identify warfare, we trace organised armed conflict between political entities. To identify atrocity, we establish scale, systematic character, civilian targeting, and the relevant forms of criminal violence. One source may answer only one of these questions.

Archaeology makes the problem especially stark because a buried body may preserve injury while losing the action, motive, and relationship that produced it. A healed fracture can indicate that a person survived an earlier trauma. A lethal wound can indicate a fatal injury. Neither trace, by itself, identifies whether the cause was interpersonal assault, a raid, a battle, punishment, accident, or ritual killing. Bone can preserve damage. It rarely preserves the full social sequence.

The difference between a healed fracture and a lethal wound is nevertheless meaningful. The first records survival and the body’s response to earlier harm; the second records an injury associated with death. Their presence in the same burial ground may invite comparison, but it does not create a population-wide measure of aggression. The number of visible injuries depends on burial practice, preservation, age, occupation, excavation, and the kinds of damage that bone can retain. A coercive act that leaves no skeletal mark may vanish from the site.

Private feeling disappears even more easily. Archaeological traces do not tell us whether a person was afraid before an injury, whether an aggressor felt anger, or whether a community regarded an act as justified. A damaged skull may establish trauma, but not the language used to authorise it. A settlement abandoned after destruction may suggest conflict, but it may also reflect disease, migration, environmental pressure, or a decision made under threat. Interpretation must move from trace to possibility without pretending that possibility is testimony.

Documents do not solve the problem; they relocate it. Morgan’s 1851 account provides offices and kinship, not a record of a particular violent encounter. Domesday provides ownership, status, tax, and service, not the private experience of the people it classifies. Archaeology may preserve a wound without a name. Administrative writing may preserve a name without a wound. The historian must ask what each kind of evidence was capable of carrying and refuse to make it carry more.

A burial site, a council, and a survey can stand at the opening of the same inquiry without forming a universal scale. The body shows one history of harm; the political account shows how a community organised relationship; the royal book shows how conquest became obligation. Each reveals a different layer of human action. None turns aggression into a single substance that can be weighed across all societies. The work begins by keeping those layers apart long enough to see how, in particular times and places, they were joined.

chapters.title: Before States: Small Communities and the Archaeological Record
chapters.markdown:
> “No such overrepresentation existed. Among those whose sex could be identified, for example, 48.7 per cent were females and 51.3 per cent were male. Furthermore, the positioning of the wounds—both frontal and back—do not support the conduct of face-to-face battles.”
>
> — Stephen J. Thorne, quoting the study, *legionmagazine.com*

At Jebel Sahaba, in the Nile Valley, the dead sharpen the question that first drew attention to them. The cemetery contains the remains of 61 individuals, and the violence associated with it has been placed within a broad range of 13,400 to 18,600 years before the present. An earlier estimate based on bone collagen from the skeleton JS 43 placed the violence at 14,979–18,568 years before the present. In the late 2010s, numerous authors rejected that date because the collagen was poorly preserved. A 2021 assessment judged that the violence might fall anywhere between 13,400 and 18,600 years before the present, while identifying 13,362–13,727 years before the present as the best estimate, based on dentine rather than collagen.

That revision leaves a long interval in which injuries were inflicted, people survived, other injuries healed, and the cemetery acquired its dead. Chronology does not dissolve the violence; it changes the temporal frame in which the violence must be understood.

A single battle is an attractive explanation for a cemetery containing projectile wounds. It supplies a compact event, a beginning and an end, and a reason for many bodies to lie together. The first interpretation of Jebel Sahaba treated it in that manner. Re-examination has made the compact story difficult to maintain. Isabelle Crevecoeur and her colleagues identified more than 100 previously undocumented healed and unhealed lesions, including several embedded stone artefacts. Working at the British Museum, where the remains were stored, they examined hundreds of bones and found previously undetected projectile impacts or broken bones in 21 individuals. Another 16 individuals had both healed and unhealed injuries.

The new examination depended partly on looking more closely. Microscopic equipment and revised techniques revealed marks that earlier excavators had missed. The change shows how the archaeological record is produced through recovery, storage, inspection, classification, and argument. A skeleton that carried no recorded wound in one account could carry several in another, not because the past had changed but because the means of seeing it had.

Most of the trauma, the reassessment reported, appears to have resulted from projectile weapons. A projectile lesion is not merely a sign of hostility in the abstract; it connects a wound to an object that travelled through space and entered a body. Yet the object does not identify the person who released it, the group to which that person belonged, or the reason for the attack. A stone point establishes a weapon more securely than it establishes a political relationship.

Healed and unhealed lesions occurred together among 41 individuals, or 67.2 per cent according to the summary of the reassessment. The coexistence of old and recent wounds points towards repeated exposure to violence. It does not mean that all 41 people endured the same series of attacks, nor does it tell us how many years separated one injury from another. It does show that the cemetery cannot be read simply as the remains of people struck down in one moment.

The study stated its conclusion plainly: “We dismiss the hypothesis that Jebel Sahaba reflects a single warfare event.” It supported “sporadic and recurrent episodes of interpersonal violence”, probably associated by the researchers with major climatic and environmental changes. Environmental change may have altered access to places, water, animals, or other necessities; the bones do not record a direct chain from a changing landscape to a particular arrow or stone.

Projectile direction offered another clue. Wounds occurred on the fronts and backs of skeletons, a pattern the study said did not support face-to-face battles. The summary of the reassessment describes the directions as suggesting raids or ambushes rather than pitched battles. That reconstruction gives movement to the violence: an attack might have caught some people from behind, or a group might have encountered danger while moving through a landscape. But “raid” and “ambush” are social descriptions, not properties visible under a microscope. They infer a mode of action from the arrangement of wounds.

The demographic pattern does not transform the cemetery into a census of victims. Among those whose sex could be identified, 48.7 per cent were female and 51.3 per cent male. The absence of an overrepresented sex was used against a simple account of a battle aimed principally at adult men. It leaves open several possibilities: people may have been attacked without selection by sex, households may have been caught in the same episode, or different episodes may have brought different kinds of victims to the same burial place. The proportions constrain interpretation while refusing to complete it.

What happened at Jebel Sahaba? The evidence supports recurrent projectile violence affecting people who included survivors of earlier injuries and people carrying injuries associated with their deaths. It supports neither a peaceful cemetery disturbed by one anomalous event nor a fully described war between named communities. The bones establish that harm occurred. The unresolved question concerns its social meaning: whether the repeated harm belonged to raids, ambushes, feuds, organised campaigns, or several forms of conflict whose traces have gathered in one place.

A raid might involve a small party striking a camp or travelling group. Warfare might involve a more durable organisation, a recognised enemy, repeated mobilisation, and purposes extending beyond one encounter. The same projectile could serve each setting. The same wound could result from a personal attack, a retaliatory expedition, or an assault conducted by people acting under collective direction. Archaeology can sometimes bring these possibilities closer together, but at Jebel Sahaba it does not choose among them decisively. The cemetery permits a history of repeated injury more securely than a history of motives, commands, or identities. The question remains open because the site records violence across lives without recording the social scale at which violence was organised.

The healed wounds and the unhealed ones belong to different temporal registers. A healed lesion is evidence that an individual survived an earlier injury long enough for the body to respond. The precise circumstances of each person’s death are not established at the cemetery. When both appear among many individuals, the site presents a population that had encountered violence at different points in its history.

At Jebel Sahaba, this pattern differs from a cemetery produced by a single attack. A single event could leave many lethal wounds, but it could explain healed injuries only if those injuries had been received before the event by people drawn from elsewhere. The reassessment instead treats the co-occurrence of old and recent lesions as evidence for sporadic and recurrent violence. The difference lies in duration. The cemetery contains bodies, but the wounds open onto lives that began before burial.

The number of recorded injuries also depends on preservation and examination. Crevecoeur’s team found more than 100 lesions that had not been documented during the first excavation in the 1960s. Twenty-one individuals had previously undetected projectile impacts or broken bones, and another 16 had both healed and unhealed injuries. These findings increase the known density of trauma, but they do not measure how often people in the wider Nile Valley were attacked. The sample is a cemetery, not a population observed continuously through time.

The question shifts when injury becomes raiding. Projectile directions may suggest raids or ambushes, and the mixture of frontal and rear wounds makes a pitched battle less persuasive. A raid, however, is already an interpretation of coordinated action. It presumes attackers who came together, a target that could be recognised, and an encounter shaped by surprise or movement. The bones can make those features plausible. They cannot name the attackers or tell us whether the same groups returned.

Warfare requires still more: some durable relationship among fighters, a conception of enemies, and a degree of planning or command. Those features need not belong to a state. Small communities can organise collective violence, and a mobile group can plan an attack without leaving fortifications or administrative records. Yet the absence of states does not make every collective attack warfare. Nor does repeated injury prove a stable military practice.

A person wounded once and a person wounded repeatedly occupy different historical positions. The first may have suffered an isolated assault or an accident that resembles one. The second survived long enough for the mark to heal and later received another injury. At Jebel Sahaba, the lesions are predominantly interpreted as violent and often projectile-related, so accidents cannot carry the whole explanation. Even so, recurrent personal exposure does not reveal whether a person lived through organised raids, local feuds, dangerous travel, or several unrelated encounters.

The 48.7 per cent female and 51.3 per cent male distribution complicates the picture of a battle without removing the possibility of organised violence. A pitched engagement between fighters might produce a different demographic pattern, but an attack on a camp, a travelling group, or a settlement could affect women and men alike. The presence of women among the injured does not establish indiscriminate targeting, and the presence of men does not establish combatant status. Sex distribution describes who appears in the cemetery; it does not assign each person a role.

Nor does the lack of a single mass burial settle the matter. The study judged a catastrophic single mass burial highly unlikely and unsupported by the archaeological and demographic evidence. That conclusion distinguishes the cemetery from a site formed in one compressed episode. It does not reduce recurrent violence to ordinary interpersonal aggression. Repeated attacks among social groups can be coordinated, feared, and strategically important even when they never become a battle in the later, more formal sense.

The contrast is between categories that overlap without merging. An injury is bodily evidence. A raid is an interpretation of an encounter. Warfare is a claim about repeated, organised relations among groups. Jebel Sahaba securely supplies the first, gives substantial support to the second, and leaves the third unsettled.

The figure of 41 people carrying both healed and unhealed lesions cannot become a rate of aggression for prehistoric communities. It records what was found among a particular group of buried individuals after preservation and examination. It excludes people whose injuries left no mark, people who died elsewhere, people who were never buried in the cemetery, and people who lived without suffering a recorded injury. The archaeological sample is evidence of harm, not a population-wide aggression index.

Several explanations remain possible, and they need not exclude one another. The first is conflict between social groups. The summary of the 2021 reassessment describes the injuries as supporting recurrent violence between groups in the Nile Valley. That reading fits projectile trauma affecting many individuals and the apparent repetition of attacks. It also keeps the scale modest enough to avoid turning every collective encounter into warfare. Groups could oppose one another without permanent armies, formal ranks, or a state.

A second explanation is mobility. If people moved between seasonal locations, water sources, hunting grounds, or sheltered places, encounters could occur at changing points across the landscape. Rear and frontal injuries might then reflect attacks on people travelling, retreating, surprised, or moving through a confined route. Mobility could also bring separate communities into contact without creating a fixed frontier. Jebel Sahaba does not establish the movements of the injured, but the possibility helps explain why repeated violence need not have centred on one permanent settlement.

A third explanation concerns resources. The Nile Valley was not a timeless abundance. The researchers associated recurrent violence with major climatic and environmental changes, and the broader archaeological interpretation proposes that altered conditions may have intensified competition. A shrinking range of accessible places could make encounters more frequent. A valued fishing ground, hunting area, or water source could become harder to share. Such pressure might encourage attacks, but it does not dictate the response. Communities may move, negotiate, divide access, or fight.

The fourth explanation is population density. More people in a limited area create more opportunities for contact, and contact creates opportunities for conflict as well as exchange. A larger population may support alliances and collective defence; it may also make disputes harder to avoid. The cemetery gives no precise count of the surrounding population and no measurement of its change. Population density therefore remains a proposed condition, not a demonstrated cause of any particular wound.

A fifth possibility is that the cemetery gathers violence selectively. People who died from injuries, or whose remains were preserved and recovered, may be overrepresented among the evidence later archaeologists examine. The site might preserve an unusual concentration of harmed people because its own history was unusual. The injuries remain important, while the question shifts from “How aggressive were these communities?” to “Why did this place contain people with this pattern of injury?”

A sixth possibility is that the repeated wounds reflect a succession of different conflicts. Climate or resource change could have altered relations over time, but the actors, targets, and immediate causes may have changed from one episode to another. A person could have been hurt in one encounter and later in another involving different opponents. The healed and unhealed lesions show recurrence more securely than continuity of enemy, policy, or purpose.

Weapons provide another line of interpretation. The dominance of projectile trauma indicates the capacity to harm from a distance. It may have allowed attackers to strike people who could not reach them, and it may have made ambushes more effective. Yet projectile points also belonged to hunting technologies. Their presence in bone demonstrates use against a person more securely than it demonstrates a specialised military class or a permanent weapon store. A tool’s lethal potential is not the same as a society’s organisation of violence.

The site’s chronology supplies a final complication. With a possible range from 13,400 to 18,600 years before the present and a best estimate of 13,362–13,727, the interval between environmental conditions, injuries, and burial remains difficult to specify. A proposed climate connection cannot be attached to a single year or attack. The landscape may have changed repeatedly, or the estimated dates may encompass more than one stage in the cemetery’s formation. The bones carry recurrence, but not a calendar of recurrence.

These explanations should remain separate. Conflict describes the immediate social relation. Mobility describes how people might have met. Resources and population density describe conditions that could increase contact or competition. Preservation and burial describe why this pattern is visible now. None alone supplies a complete account, and the evidence becomes stronger when these questions are not forced into one cause.

The need for such separation is clear at Crow Creek in South Dakota, where archaeological work involved not only bones and trauma but consultation over their handling. Before excavation could proceed, the Corps of Engineers and the University of South Dakota Archaeology Laboratory team consulted the Crow Creek Sioux Reservation Tribal Council and representatives of the Mandan and Arikara peoples, whose communities were then based mostly on the Fort Berthold Indian Reservation in North Dakota.

The consultation changed the conditions of study. The researchers agreed to the tribal council’s request that the remains stay within South Dakota for the entire period of examination. They also agreed that, after study, the remains should be reburied at the Crow Creek site, described in the account as the place where the families had lived and died.

The recorded episode is brief. It does not provide the number or identities of the remains, the date or duration of the study, the circumstances of death, or the condition of the bones. It records an agreement about custody and return. Archaeological investigation here was a negotiated activity involving the Corps of Engineers, the University of South Dakota team, the tribal council, and Mandan and Arikara representatives. That agreement belongs in a history of evidence because evidence is shaped by what happens to bodies after death. The location of remains, permission to examine them, and the agreement to rebury them affect what can be learned and how the dead are treated.

At Jebel Sahaba, the remains were examined at the British Museum and new techniques altered the recorded pattern of injury. At Crow Creek, the terms of study were shaped through consultation and a commitment to keep the remains in South Dakota. The two cases provide different kinds of information, but both show that archaeology joins bodily traces to present-day choices.

Crow Creek places a limit on the historian’s freedom to treat remains as material detached from living communities. The dead can be evidence of an old attack, a burial practice, or a population’s history, but they are also ancestors claimed by particular peoples. Consultation does not erase the violence that archaeology may investigate. It determines how investigation proceeds.

Jebel Sahaba asks whether recurring projectile injuries belong to raiding, warfare, or smaller attacks. Crow Creek adds another question: who has the right to decide how the dead enter that inquiry? One addresses the organisation of ancient violence; the other addresses the organisation of modern knowledge about violence. Neither can be answered by counting wounds alone.

The most revealing phrase in the Jebel Sahaba account may be the study’s statement that “a catastrophic single mass burial is highly unlikely and not supported by the archaeological evidence and the demographic analysis.” Its force lies in what it removes. The cemetery need not be a single battlefield. The sentence leaves a field of recurrent episodes, projectile attacks, and social groups whose names and purposes remain unknown.

The second important phrase is “sporadic and recurrent episodes of interpersonal violence.” The adjectives pull in different directions. “Sporadic” resists the picture of continuous war; “recurrent” resists the picture of an isolated quarrel. “Interpersonal” keeps attention on people harming people, while the reference to social groups opens the possibility of collective conflict. The wording is careful because the bones require care.

A third phrase, “raids or ambushes, rather than pitched battles,” offers a social scale without pretending to provide an army. A raid can be organised and consequential while remaining small. An ambush can involve planning without a permanent command structure. Neither term requires a state, and neither proves one. The vocabulary marks a plausible form of conflict while preserving uncertainty about how groups were constituted and how they acted.

The healed wound is the quietest piece of evidence and perhaps the most significant. It carries time inside the skeleton. Someone survived an earlier injury; later, that person entered a cemetery with another lesion or with a body that bore the marks of violence. That history supports recurrence, but it cannot tell us whether the earlier and later attacks were connected. The body records sequence more readily than it records organisation.

For that reason, prehistoric evidence can distinguish repeated harm from a single event more securely than it can distinguish recurrent raiding from organised war. It can establish that violence reached many individuals, that projectiles were used, and that some victims had survived previous injuries. The patterns are compatible with ambushes or raids, but at Jebel Sahaba they do not name a commander, identify an alliance, or establish the rules by which fighters were gathered and released.

The uncertainty does not reduce the site to silence. Jebel Sahaba reveals a community of dead and injured people who lived through a period in which projectile violence recurred. Crow Creek reveals that the study of violent remains is governed by consultation, custody, and obligations to descendants. Between them lies a history of harm that is substantial without being convertible into a universal measure of aggressiveness.

A wound is not a war. A cemetery records the dead without functioning as a census. The archaeological record becomes most intelligible when it allows both statements to stand.

chapters.title: Cities, Kings, and the Invention of Organized War
chapters.markdown:
The text, written in early Sumerian cuneiform, alternates between mythic and historical language. It celebrates Eannatum’s conquest but also details treaties, field boundaries, and temple endowments. That mixture shows how early rulers used writing and art to claim divine legitimacy — to turn politics into religion.

The stele begins with a quarrel over ground. Lagash and Umma were neighbouring city-states in Mesopotamia, and the disputed ground was fertile farmland between their territories. The record does not give the quarrel a single beginning or preserve the full settlement that followed, but it presents the conflict as more than a clash between armed men. Eannatum of Lagash appears as a ruler who made a territorial claim, led force against the claim’s opponents, and then fixed the meaning of victory in stone at Girsu, the main religious centre of his realm.

The monument belongs to a world of independent cities rather than a single Mesopotamian kingdom. Lagash had a city, a ruling house, a patron deity, fields, temples, and boundaries; Umma possessed its own claims and interests. The ground between them could be fought over because it was already being treated as something that could belong to a political community. A wound at Jebel Sahaba marks violence on a body. The stele marks violence as an act concerning land, cities, gods, and the authority of a named ruler.

Eannatum sought to settle the conflict permanently, “with force, and with art.” The phrase joins two actions often separated in accounts of early warfare. Force changes the immediate balance between opponents. Art gives the change a public form that can outlast the fighters who produced it. The stele presents Lagash’s defeat of Umma as an event with a rightful owner, a territorial consequence, and a warning attached to it. Its inscription says that Ningirsu, the patron god of Lagash, “granted Eannatum victory” over Umma.

The wording places the ruler inside a chain of authorisation. Eannatum acts, but his success is not represented as an achievement produced by human strength alone. Ningirsu grants the victory; Eannatum receives and exercises it; Lagash gains the authority that the monument records. The claim does not tell us how the fighting was organised in every practical detail, how many people took part, or how the opposing side understood the outcome. It tells us how the Lagashite monument wanted the outcome understood. The stele is a public argument made from the victor’s side.

Its images place Eannatum at the head of a disciplined formation. He leads “a phalanx of soldiers, spears bristling in a tight formation.” The king is larger than the other figures and walks at the front, trampling enemies underfoot. Beneath him lie the defeated, while vultures carry severed heads. The scene turns a violent encounter into an ordered procession: the living army advances, the king leads, the enemy falls, and the birds complete the work of death.

The soldiers’ formation supplies a visual grammar for organised force. Spears are not scattered among unrelated individuals. They are held in a common line. The king is not one fighter among others. He is enlarged and placed at the head, where command becomes visible. The defeated are rendered as a mass beneath that movement, their bodies contributing to the contrast between Lagashite order and Umma’s collapse. The image cannot establish the actual number of soldiers, the duration of the engagement, or the precise tactics used. It establishes that the monument associated victory with disciplined collective action under a ruler.

Eannatum’s position at the front also makes the army’s violence a political act. The king does not appear merely as the strongest combatant. His body organises the scene. The soldiers follow a direction that his position makes intelligible, while the dead confirm the consequence of his command. A ruler represented as leading a formation can claim more than courage. He can claim that the city’s force is gathered through him and that the city’s success is embodied in his office.

The birds carrying severed heads sharpen the image’s purpose. Their presence is “a grim reminder that the gods, too, consume the dead.” Human victory is folded into a larger sacred order. The enemy’s destruction becomes evidence that Lagash’s cause has prevailed in the world governed by its gods. Violence against the defeated is not shown as an eruption that escaped control. It is arranged as the visible result of an authorised struggle.

The monument’s second visual register changes the scale without changing the result. Ningirsu strides forward holding a net filled with captives, while Ninhursag stands behind him. The god’s net gathers the defeated in a single object. Captivity, which on a battlefield would involve separate bodies and practical acts of restraint, becomes in divine hands a sign of total power. The captives do not appear as independent opponents with claims of their own. They are enclosed within the god’s emblem and carried by the meaning of his victory.

Ninhursag, “mother of the gods,” reinforces the cosmic scale of the scene. Her presence places the god’s act within a divine family and gives the victory a setting larger than the dispute over farmland. Earthly conflict is made to resemble heavenly struggle. The image does not dissolve territory into myth; it gives territory a sacred frame. The fields between Lagash and Umma become ground over which divine favour can be declared.

After the victory it describes, the stele was erected in Girsu as both record and warning. A monument in a religious centre could address more than the people who had witnessed the fighting. It could present the settlement to worshippers, officials, rivals, and later generations through the same carved surfaces. The warning was attached to a durable object placed where Lagash’s religious and political claims met, without relying on a messenger carrying the king’s words to every border.

The warning’s terms are uncompromising: the gods of Lagash protect their city, and trespassers will be destroyed. Here the conflict over land becomes a claim about the kind of act an incursion would be. A rival crossing a boundary would not merely challenge a local possession. The rival would enter a space guarded by a god and defended by a ruler whose victory had already been authorised. The monument converts a disputed border into a test of legitimacy.

The surviving account leaves the precise settlement between Lagash and Umma unknown, along with the exact boundaries and later political consequences. The stele’s force lies elsewhere. It shows a ruler joining battlefield action to a language of fields, treaties, temples, and divine protection. Conflict becomes durable when the act of defeating an opponent is attached to an office, a territory, and a public account of rightful order.

This monument belongs beside, rather than above, the evidence of earlier violence. The healed and unhealed lesions at Jebel Sahaba support repeated episodes of projectile violence, and the reassessment associated with Isabelle Crevecoeur and her colleagues rejected the idea of a single warfare event. That evidence reveals recurrence and injury. The stele adds a named authority and a declared cause. It does not prove that earlier communities lacked organisation, nor that every later battle was governed by the same form of kingship. It shows what changes when a ruler can make a public claim about why force was used and what territory force was meant to secure.

The inscription and images do this work together. If the carved text concerned only the ruler’s bravery, it would leave the land in the background. If the boundary claim appeared without the army, it would lack the visible means by which the claim was enforced. If the god appeared without captives or fallen enemies, divine favour would remain a general blessing. Instead, the stele binds the elements into one account: land is disputed, a king leads soldiers, a god grants victory, enemies are overcome, and a monument warns those who might challenge the result.

The text moves between registers that modern readers might separate. It celebrates Eannatum’s conquest while also detailing treaties, field boundaries, and temple endowments. The shift from conquest to administration is not a retreat from violence. It shows the work violence is made to perform after the fighting. A victory must be placed somewhere, assigned a boundary, related to obligations, and connected to the institutions that maintain a city’s sacred and material life.

A treaty belongs to a relationship between political parties. A field boundary gives an abstract claim a location. A temple endowment links property and religious service. These are different kinds of statement, but the stele places them within one political vocabulary. The ruler who claims victory also claims knowledge of the land, the authority to define its limits, and the right to direct resources towards temples. Force appears not as a separate activity carried out by men who disappear when the battle ends, but as part of a wider claim to govern.

The mixture of mythic and administrative language allowed early rulers to claim divine legitimacy and “turn politics into religion.” The monument shows that the two domains were already being presented as inseparable. The god authorised the ruler; the ruler defended the city; the city’s fields and temples gave the claim material form. Religious language did not float above administration. It helped explain why boundaries, endowments, and military victory belonged together.

The words “granted Eannatum victory” concentrate this relationship in a few terms. Victory is not described as an accidental result of strength or numbers. It is granted. The recipient is not the city in an impersonal sense but Eannatum, whose name gives the act a human bearer. The opponent is Umma, a political community rather than an unnamed crowd. The sentence distributes agency among god, ruler, city, and rival. It also makes the ruler’s success evidence of a proper order that precedes and outlasts the moment of combat.

That language can legitimate a ruler after the danger has passed. A battlefield victory may be contested by those who suffered it, by those who paid for it, or by officials who must administer its consequences. A sacred inscription narrows the acceptable account. To dispute Eannatum’s victory is, within the monument’s own logic, to question the judgement of Ningirsu. To cross the protected boundary is to oppose both Lagash and its god. The political claim gains weight by being stated in terms that a human rival cannot easily answer without appearing to resist the divine order itself.

The visual programme repeats the same argument without relying on literacy. Eannatum’s enlarged body makes hierarchy visible. His soldiers’ spears form a single bristling field. The dead are below, and the vultures carry their heads away. On the other side, Ningirsu holds the net of captives. The image does not distribute attention evenly between victor and defeated. It gives shape to the victor’s command and compresses the enemy into the consequences of disobedience.

The net changes the meaning of capture. A field of prisoners could represent a temporary condition produced by battle. A god holding prisoners in a net represents the ability to gather and contain them as a group. The net makes domination look total even when the actual number and identity of captives remain unknown. Its mesh is a sign of political reach: those who have been defeated cannot stand apart from the result or return to the status they possessed before the encounter.

Ninhursag’s position behind Ningirsu adds a second form of confirmation. The divine scene is not a solitary display of force. It is witnessed and supported within a sacred order. The goddess’s presence strengthens the sense that the victory is not a private preference of the patron deity but an event with a wider cosmic setting. Human war is represented as a reflection of divine order, so that the ruler’s territorial claim appears to have a counterpart beyond the human world.

The scene’s religious certainty should not be mistaken for certainty about the historical event. The stele does not preserve the full wording of every inscription for us here, the original arrangement of all its images, or the names and number of the dead and captives. Its assertions remain assertions made by Lagash. But assertions can themselves be historical evidence. They reveal the categories through which a ruler wanted conflict remembered: conquest, boundary, treaty, endowment, god, king, captive, and warning.

That vocabulary also places limits on what the monument allows us to see. The people of Umma appear as trespassers and defeated bodies, not as a community with an argument over land. The stele does not give their account of the boundary, nor does it record whether they accepted the settlement described by their opponent. Its silence is part of its political design. The monument is not trying to preserve a balanced negotiation. It is trying to make Lagash’s position durable.

Durability depends on more than the object’s survival. The monument links three kinds of persistence. The inscription preserves words after the immediate event. The image preserves the arrangement of king, army, god, and captive. The place at Girsu situates the claim within a religious centre where the victory can be encountered as part of the city’s ordered world. A ruler’s coercive act becomes harder to detach from legitimacy when these forms reinforce one another.

The same connection can be seen in the mention of temple endowments. A military victory is translated into an allocation of resources. The ruler who defeats an enemy can present himself as the person who restores or enlarges the material basis of worship. The temple’s endowment helps confirm that the king’s action has produced an order worthy of divine maintenance. War, property, and devotion become stages in a single account of rule.

Territory gives that account a measurable surface. A god may authorise a claim, but a field boundary tells officials and cultivators where the claim begins and ends. The document’s administrative language performs a different task from its battle scenes. The images establish power through bodies and weapons. The boundary language translates that power into a geography that can be marked, remembered, and perhaps enforced through later decisions. Public authority becomes durable when it can move from the spectacle of victory to the management of land.

Force gains a longer life when it is written into categories that officials can apply and communities can recognise. The stele’s surviving account is a monument of victory and divine legitimacy, not a comprehensive survey.

What does a monument preserve when the ruler who commissioned it is gone? It may preserve the ruler’s name, the claimed enemy, the sacred authority invoked, and the territory described. It may preserve an official vocabulary through which later claims can be made to resemble earlier ones. The object cannot itself patrol a boundary, feed soldiers, or adjudicate a treaty. It can supply a precedent and a public form for those activities, especially when it stands within a religious and political centre.

The answer depends on the office attached to the words. Eannatum’s claim is not presented as the opinion of a private landholder. He speaks through kingship, and his victory is placed within the protection of Ningirsu and the life of Lagash. An office allows a personal act to be described as a public act. The ruler’s campaign concerns the city; the city’s god authorises the ruler; the city’s fields become the object of defence. This circulation gives coercion a collective name.

A boundary can be administered only if someone is empowered to identify trespass, hear a dispute, or punish a refusal. The stele does not preserve the procedures by which every such decision was made, and its account does not reveal the full institutional life of Lagash or Umma. It does show the vocabulary in which such procedures could be justified. Treaties, field boundaries, and temple endowments belong to repeated acts of allocation, recognition, collection, and enforcement.

A ruler’s coercive claim becomes durable through a sequence that begins before the monument and continues after it. First, a territorial dispute identifies a piece of land as politically significant. Second, armed force changes the immediate position of the rival. Third, the ruler attributes victory to a god and presents the army’s discipline as evidence of legitimate command. Fourth, writing and images fix the outcome at Girsu. Finally, boundaries, treaties, and endowments give the victory administrative forms that can be invoked beyond the original battle.

Each step narrows the distance between violence and order. The field is not merely seized; it is described. The enemy is not merely beaten; the enemy becomes a trespasser. The ruler’s success is presented as the receipt of divine favour, and the monument warns. The record does not tell us how effectively this sequence worked in every later dispute, but it shows the components of a public claim that could outlast the event that produced it.

The question left by Lagash and Umma is larger than whether cities fought more often than small communities. Did the city create organised violence, or did it give older forms of conflict a new language and a longer institutional life? The stele makes both possibilities visible. Its phalanx, royal leadership, captives, and territorial administration suggest collective force coordinated through a ruler. Its existence also shows that the most durable transformation may have occurred after the fighting, when victory was converted into a claim about land, gods, and lawful authority.

The answer cannot be extracted from this monument alone. Its date is not established in the evidence used here, the precise territorial settlement is unknown, and no second independent early-state case has been placed beside it in a way that would support a general law. The stele is powerful evidence for what Lagash’s ruler claimed and how that claim was composed. It is not a measuring instrument for all cities. Still, it reveals a pathway by which organised violence could emerge as a public institution.

Agricultural land supplied a reason for conflict. A city supplied a community in whose name the claim could be made. A ruler supplied command. A god supplied authorisation. Writing supplied continuity. Boundaries supplied a practical object. None of these elements alone constitutes warfare, but together they make force legible as a duty of government.

The process could also redirect violence. Once a ruler claimed responsibility for defending territory, private attacks on neighbours could be treated as trespass against the city. Once captives and fields entered a public vocabulary, the defeated could be classified and managed rather than simply killed or dispersed. A state’s ability to gather soldiers and resources enlarged the possible scale of harm, but the same power could define agreements, protect boundaries, or settle claims.

The monument records coercion most vividly; its administrative language leaves room for forms of order that are not reducible to battle. That is why the phrase “invention of organised war” requires care. The stele supplies evidence of organisation in representation: soldiers march in formation, a king leads, a god gathers captives, and a city’s territory is defended. It does not allow every feature of the historical army to be reconstructed. We do not know from these passages how troops were recruited, how long they served, how supplies moved, or how command operated away from the king’s presence. The image proves that organised force was a central public idea. It does not by itself provide the whole army.

A more cautious mechanism begins with the land. When two cities treat the same farmland as part of their political territories, a dispute can be framed as a public injury rather than a private quarrel. A ruler can then gather armed men under the city’s name. If the ruler wins, the victory can be linked to a god whose protection explains the outcome. The ruler can commission a monument in a religious centre, where the victory becomes visible and memorable. Writing can specify boundaries and obligations, while images show the consequences of resistance. The original act of force is thereby converted into a continuing claim over territory.

Cities did not need to produce the human ability to injure one another for this process to begin. They supplied offices, places, resources, and records through which injury could be organised and justified. Their walls, temples, fields, labour, and taxes may have enabled larger concentrations of force, as the broader pattern of early urban societies suggests. Yet the Lagashite monument cannot establish that every city followed the same path or that urban life uniformly increased violence.

The stele’s significance lies in the change of register. A body can bear the mark of a projectile. A battlefield can contain the dead. A ruler’s monument can say who was authorised to cause those deaths, which land they secured, and what order the dead are meant to confirm. That transformation shows how a city and a king could make conflict into a durable public claim about territory, legitimacy, and order, while leaving violence contingent and forms of harm unequal.

chapters.title: Empires and the Management of Difference
chapters.markdown:
> “The text, written in early Sumerian cuneiform, alternates between mythic and historical language. It celebrates Eannatum’s conquest but also details treaties, field boundaries, and temple endowments. That mix of myth and administration shows how early rulers used writing and art to claim divine legitimacy — to turn politics into religion.”

The Lachish relief begins with the position from which the city’s inhabitants are to be seen. Sennacherib sits on an ornately decorated throne in the Assyrian camp, and the plunder of Lachish passes before him. The inscription beside the throne identifies the scene: “Sennacherib, king of the world, king of Assyria, sat on the throne as the plunder of Lachish passed before him.” The words settle what the image alone might leave uncertain. This is Lachish, not an interchangeable conquest; this is the king receiving the result of a siege, not merely inspecting a military camp.

The throne fixes the centre of the composition. Around it, the movement of goods and people acquires direction. Plunder is not simply taken; it is brought before the ruler, arranged as evidence of his reach. The city has been transformed into a procession towards the king. What was once held by Lachish now confirms Assyrian possession, and the relief makes that transfer visible on the palace wall. The throne is more than furniture. It is the place where force becomes royal achievement.

The scene’s violence is not confined to the battlefield. Outside the city, three people, described by George Heath-Whyte as likely government officials or military commanders, are impaled on stakes for rebellion against Assyria. Two others are shown being flayed alive. The passage does not identify them by name, and the relief cannot tell us whether each punishment occurred exactly as depicted. It does show punishment placed within the same visual field as siege and plunder. The conquered city is represented through several consequences of resistance: defeat, the removal of goods, the exposure of bodies, and the submission of what remains to the king.

Heath-Whyte writes that the scenes were likely intended to ridicule the king of Judah and remind viewers of what awaited those who attempted rebellion. The interpretation rests on the relation between the acts shown and the palace in which they were carved. A punishment outside Lachish could be witnessed by people near the city. A punishment carved in Sennacherib’s palace addressed visitors who entered the Assyrian court, officials who moved through it, and subjects who encountered the king’s image in a setting organised around royal power. The relief carried the city into the palace and made its destruction part of the ruler’s public identity.

The final scene separates the king from the immediate physical work of violence without separating him from responsibility for its meaning. Soldiers, officials, captives, and plunder occupy the field of action; Sennacherib occupies the position of judgement and possession. The relief gives the king distance from injury while preserving his proximity to its rewards. Its arrangement also changes the scale of the event. Lachish was a particular city in Judah. On the palace wall it becomes a lesson about Assyrian rule. The inscription calls Sennacherib “king of the world”, placing a local siege within a universal claim. The city’s fate is made to stand for the fate of any place that resists.

The passage describing the relief links this warning to Sennacherib’s failure to take Jerusalem. The king of Judah could be ridiculed because one city had resisted while another, Lachish, had been captured and displayed. A local defeat thus became an imperial message.

The relief joins three kinds of statement. It records an event by naming Lachish. It interprets the event by placing plunder before Sennacherib. It threatens beyond the event by presenting mutilated bodies as the consequence of rebellion. Written words and carved forms do different work, but neither is incidental. The small caption identifies the city; the throne identifies the recipient; the punishments identify the cost. A monument that shows only battle might celebrate victory. This one organises victory into a grammar of submission.

Its power lies partly in the fact that the viewer is not asked to choose between administrative control and terror. The palace wall accommodates both. Goods must be gathered and counted, people must be classified as rebels or subjects, and the ruler must be represented as the recipient of what the army has secured. The scene makes coercion legible through order. Bodies, objects, and titles occupy their assigned places. The horror is not an interruption of imperial administration. It has been given a place within it.

The inscription also exposes a tension between records. Sennacherib’s own written accounts do not mention Lachish by name, while the caption beside the throne identifies it with certainty. Biblical passages, including 2 Chronicles 32:9 and 2 Kings 18:14, mention the siege and communications between Hezekiah in Jerusalem and Sennacherib at Lachish. The relief’s visual programme preserves a particular version of the event, while its caption opens the scene to a wider historical reconstruction. The evidence joins palace art, inscription, and biblical narrative without making them identical.

The king’s throne is stable because the city has been made unstable. Lachish appears not as a political community with its own internal life but as a source of plunder, punishment, and warning. The captives and the punished are present, but their names, purposes, and accounts are not. They have been turned into signs.

The question left by the relief is how a ruler could make siege, plunder, and punishment serve as an image of order rather than disorder. The answer appears in the arrangement itself, but only in the language of the palace.

The capture of Lachish was an act of war, yet the relief does not preserve the whole course of the siege. It does not give the precise date or duration, the number of people taken, or the route by which plunder and deportees left the city. Its sequence is compressed into visible consequences: a city is attacked, its people are punished, and its wealth is brought to Sennacherib. Between those points lies the labour of conquest, but the monument’s purpose is not to narrate every step.

What did the relief make punishment accomplish? If the impaled people were officials or commanders, as Heath-Whyte suggests, their bodies could be read as a judgement on those who had represented Lachish. If they were made examples for rebellion, the image addressed future behaviour as much as past conduct. The punishment was directed at the defeated, but its imagined audience extended beyond them. Assyria’s violence was local in execution and imperial in address.

The relief’s warning may have worked because it combined certainty with theatrical distance. The viewer saw the consequence but not the private decision that preceded it. No inner motive is available for the people outside the city, and no exact legal procedure is shown. What appears is the completed judgement. The king’s authority is represented as already settled, while the rebels are fixed in the posture assigned to them. The monument cannot tell us whether every punishment happened exactly as represented. Nor can it identify the two people who were flayed or establish how many others were deported or plundered. It gives strong evidence for an imperial language of exemplary punishment and royal possession, but weaker evidence for the full social experience of Lachish’s capture.

The city’s fate raises a problem about the relationship between destruction and rule. A punitive display can deter resistance, but deterrence is not administration. Assyria needed more than fear to hold territories, move goods, communicate orders, and define obligations. The relief presents the moment when force becomes visible, not all the quieter work required after force has succeeded. Its silence about local intermediaries is significant. The imperial centre is crowded with the king’s image and nearly empty of conquered political voices.

The Cyrus Cylinder, composed in a different imperial setting, offers a sharply different surface. Without stakes, flayed bodies, or plunder passing before a throne, it speaks through divine choice, peaceful entry, sanctuary protection, and relief from an oppressive yoke. Lachish is presented as a conquered city made into a warning; Babylon is presented as a city entered by a ruler who calls himself a harbinger of peace.

The cylinder begins by assigning the initiative to Marduk. In the damaged passage translated by Robert William Rogers, the preceding ruler is associated with improper rites, halted offerings, interference within sanctuaries, and a burden imposed on the population. Marduk then “took pity” on the people of Sumer and Akkad, inspected the countries, and sought an upright king. He “took the hand of Cyrus, king of the city of Anshan,” proclaimed him for kingship, and ordered him to go to Babylon. The account turns conquest into a response to divine diagnosis. Cyrus does not appear first as an invader who has overcome a city; he appears as the ruler selected to repair one.

That repair is stated in political as well as religious terms. Cyrus says, “When I went as harbinger of peace i[nt]o Babylon I founded my sovereign residence within the palace amid celebration and rejoicing.” His troops, he continues, were marching peaceably, and Sumer and Akkad had nothing to fear. He sought the safety of Babylon and all its sanctuaries. The population, described as having endured a yoke “not decreed for them,” received relief from its weariness.

The wording does not remove empire from the scene. Cyrus names himself king of the universe, great king, powerful king, king of Babylon, king of Sumer and Akkad, and king of the four quarters of the world. Peace appears inside an assertion of universal sovereignty. The inscription’s accommodation is not an alternative to imperial power; it is the form in which that power wishes to be recognised.

Lachish and Babylon differ in the violence they display, but also in the political problem they address. The Lachish relief speaks to rebellion through punishment. The Cyrus Cylinder speaks to legitimacy through rescue. One presents a ruler seated over the results of force; the other presents a ruler whose entry is peaceful because the previous order has already been judged defective. The first says that resistance will be broken. The second says that submission can be experienced as release.

The difference may reflect the needs of the records rather than a simple difference between Assyrian and Persian character. Sennacherib’s relief is a palace composition centred on a siege and its plunder. The cylinder is an inscription in which Cyrus presents his kingship through Babylonian religious and political vocabulary. A monument that commemorates punishment will emphasise the consequences of defiance. An inscription that establishes a new ruler in Babylon will emphasise the easing of burdens. Each document selects a useful register.

The Cyrus Cylinder’s account of Marduk’s choice binds accommodation to divine legitimation. Cyrus is said to shepherd the people in justice and righteousness, but he is first placed in that role by Marduk. The ruler’s benevolence is not described as a private disposition. It is a public qualification for kingship. He is acceptable because the god has chosen him, because his actions please the god, and because his rule answers the disorder attributed to the predecessor.

The cylinder makes the population visible in a way the Lachish relief does not. The people of Babylon are said to have endured a yoke, and Cyrus says he soothed their weariness. Their experience is still narrated by the conqueror, not recorded in their own words, and the damaged passage leaves several details uncertain. Yet they are not merely plunder or bodies. They are a population whose condition helps justify the transfer of sovereignty. The ruler’s claim depends on presenting their relief as both a divine purpose and an imperial achievement.

Sanctuaries receive similar attention. The preceding ruler is accused of interrupting rites and interfering within holy places. Cyrus seeks the safety of Babylon and all its sanctuaries. Accommodation claims to preserve proper relations between ruler, city, population, and gods. The new empire presents itself as protective because it recognises local sacred order, or at least speaks in the language by which that order is publicly understood.

A conqueror who protects sanctuaries still controls them. A king who frees a population from an unwanted yoke still identifies himself as king of the universe. The cylinder does not imagine Babylon outside imperial hierarchy. It makes the city’s safety evidence that hierarchy is functioning properly. Peaceful troops, rejoicing, and sanctuary protection demonstrate the quality of Cyrus’s sovereignty rather than limiting it.

This is where the two records meet. Sennacherib’s relief makes violence a warning about the fate of communities that resist imperial power. Cyrus’s cylinder makes protection a reason for communities to accept imperial power. The instruments differ: impalement and flaying in one record, peace and relief in the other. The political grammar is related. In each case, the ruler claims the right to define what the conquered city needs and to present his intervention as the answer.

The Lachish relief does not represent accommodation because its selected episode is punitive. The Cyrus Cylinder does not represent the absence of force because its peaceful entry is a claim made within a declaration of universal kingship. The documents cannot be placed on a single scale from cruelty to kindness. They preserve different imperial solutions to difference: break resistance where it is dangerous, and preserve or restore local forms where they can support obedience.

A city may be threatened by the sight of punished rebels. Another may be reassured by the promise that its sanctuaries will be safe. Neither response requires the empire to abandon its claim over the city. The choice between them can depend on the condition of the territory, the form of the local elite, the religious vocabulary available to the ruler, and the audience the monument addresses. Lachish is shown as an example to others. Babylon is described as a community whose acceptance can be cultivated.

That cultivation should not be mistaken for equality. Cyrus’s inscription places Babylon within a hierarchy extending from Anshan to the four quarters of the world. The population is relieved because the king says so, and the previous ruler’s wrongdoing is defined through the new ruler’s account. Accommodation remains paternal and imperial. It offers protection from disorder while preserving the right to determine what counts as order.

The same asymmetry appears in the Assyrian scene. Sennacherib’s authority is not shown as a negotiation with Lachish. The city’s political meaning has been absorbed into the king’s victory. Yet the relief’s purpose is not only to celebrate destruction. It also makes future administration possible by showing the consequences of refusing the king’s terms. Terror communicates an expectation: local power may continue only within imperial limits.

The earlier stele of Lagash and Umma joined battle scenes to field boundaries, treaties, and temple endowments. The Lachish relief extends that movement from an act of force towards a durable claim, but on a larger imperial stage. Its inscription identifies the conquered city and the ruler who receives its wealth. The Cyrus Cylinder extends the same movement through another register. It converts the arrival of a conqueror into a claim of sacred and civic order. In both cases, the document gives the event a usable political shape.

The difference between coercion and accommodation is real at the level of experience. Being impaled, flayed, dispossessed, or driven from a city is not equivalent to having a sanctuary protected or a burden reduced. A warning carved on a palace wall and a claim of peaceful entry are not interchangeable kinds of evidence. At the level of imperial rule, however, both can make the transfer and maintenance of authority intelligible.

A punitive spectacle may narrow the space available to local leaders. A promise of sanctuary protection may widen it, provided that local rites and officials support the imperial order. The first can suppress rebellion; the second can recruit cooperation. An empire can require both, using force against a city that resists and accommodation towards communities whose cooperation reduces the cost of rule.

The Cyrus Cylinder’s language makes this flexibility clear. Cyrus’s troops are described as marching peaceably, while the king also claims the title “king of the universe” and the authority to found his residence in Babylon. Peace is not the condition in which imperial sovereignty disappears. It is the condition in which sovereignty can appear legitimate. The king’s ability to protect the city depends on the city’s incorporation into his rule.

The claim that benevolence and terror are opposing systems has a clear appeal. A ruler who flays rebels appears to belong to a political world unlike that of a ruler who promises sanctuary protection. Punishment injures bodies; accommodation preserves institutions. One creates fear, while the other seeks consent. The distinction should remain. The Lachish captives and the Babylonian population should not be placed under a single description of imperial conduct. Opposition becomes misleading when it suggests that an empire must choose one technique and reject the other.

The Lachish relief itself is an administrative image: it identifies the site, names the ruler, locates the plunder, and assigns punishment a public purpose. The Cyrus Cylinder’s benevolence is an imperial claim: it names Cyrus king of the universe, attributes his selection to Marduk, and places peaceful troops within Babylon. In both records, rule is organised through a story about who may command, who needs protection, and what happens when the existing order is judged illegitimate.

Terror and accommodation can address different audiences. The mutilated bodies on the Assyrian palace wall speak to those who might contemplate rebellion. The cylinder’s language about sanctuaries and relief speaks to Babylonian religious and civic expectations. A ruler could frighten a military opponent while reassuring officials and inhabitants whose cooperation was needed. The absence of one register from a document does not prove its absence from imperial practice. Nor does accommodation mean that conquered communities retained independent power.

Cyrus’s protection of Babylonian sanctuaries may have helped preserve local religious life, but it did so within a new sovereignty. The city’s rites become evidence that the new king governs properly. Local difference is allowed to remain where it can be made compatible with imperial authority. When difference is treated as a source of rebellion, as in the Lachish scene, the imperial answer is harsher.
